extracted.intended_audience: literary readers, artists and art-critics, and general public interested in Whitman's essays and lectures
extracted.subtask_short: literary essays on art and Lincoln
extracted.subtask_description: A collection of Walt Whitman's essays/lecture excerpts and letters discussing aesthetics (representation of sex and the nude), social implications (women's rights), and a memorial lecture on Abraham Lincoln's death and its national/artistic significance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assumption of the sanity of birth, Nature and humanity
rubrics_metrics.description: "the assumption of the sanity of birth, Nature and humanity, is the key to any true theory of life and the universe... it is, and must inevitably be, the only key to 'Leaves of Grass'"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whitman frames this assumption as the foundational principle for his poetry: maintaining these particular verses uncompromisingly for over twenty years; it is the 'enclosing basis of everything' for his work and must underlie interpretation and creation of poems in that book.

rubrics_metrics.name: Redeem sexual subject from disreputable treatment
rubrics_metrics.description: "redeeming of this subject from its hitherto relegation to the tongues and pens of blackguards, and boldly putting it... in the demesne of poetry and sanity--as something not in itself gross or impure, but entirely consistent with highest manhood and womanhood"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sexuality and its representation should be treated by serious poetry and art as natural, dignified, and integral to humanity, not as base or merely prurient material; artists should assert such themes 'openly, joyously, proudly, without shame or the need of shame.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Representation of motherhood/fatherhood/sexuality without shame
rubrics_metrics.description: "motherhood, fatherhood, sexuality, and all that belongs to them, can be asserted... 'without shame or the need of shame' from the highest artistic and human considerations"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Artistic and literary works addressing parental and sexual themes should present them reverently and integrally to human life, so that families and society 'bless and thank' the portrayal rather than recoil from it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conventional/prurient treatment of sex hinders women's eligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: "To the movement for the eligibility and entrance of women amid new spheres... the current prurient, conventional treatment of sex is the main formidable obstacle."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Social progress for women's rights requires replacing prurient, conventional discourse about sex with 'a sensible, philosophic, democratic method'; artistic treatment participates in this social reform.

rubrics_metrics.name: Right of the nude in art if by trained artists with noble ethic
rubrics_metrics.description: "it is necessary for the future of English art and of English morality that the right of the nude to a place in our galleries should be boldly asserted; it must, however, be the nude as represented by thoroughly trained artists, and with a pure and noble ethic purpose."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Admission of nude figures into galleries is advocated, but only where representation is skillful and guided by high ethical aims; poor or immodest portraits are the real fault, not nudity per se.

rubrics_metrics.name: Human form as standard of beauty; familiarity required
rubrics_metrics.description: "The human form, male and female, is the type and standard of all beauty of form and proportion, and it is necessary to be thoroughly familiar with it in order safely to judge of all beauty which consists of form and proportion."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Artists, the public, and especially women should become familiar with ideal forms to recognize perfection and avoid artificial distortions (examples given: tight-lacing, scandalous dress, foot-torturing boots and high heels). Familiarity serves public taste and health.

rubrics_metrics.name: Familiar public display of tasteful nudes reduces prurient curiosity
rubrics_metrics.description: "The effect of nude representation of women upon young men is unwholesome, but it would not be so if such works were admitted without question into our galleries, and became thoroughly familiar to them."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whitman (via the Rathbone argument) holds that concealment breeds prurient curiosity and evil imaginings; normalized, tasteful exposure in art would educate the eye and reduce unhealthy curiosity (contrasts theatre partial exposure with full, familiar nudes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Indecency arises in the beholder's thought, not in clear-aimed representation
rubrics_metrics.description: "No, it is not the picture or nude statue or text, with clear aim, that is indecent; it is the beholder's own thought, inference, distorted construction."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Moral judgment should focus on intent and quality of representation and on the viewer's response; 'true modesty' is valuable but pretended modesty is false. Whitman invokes a scriptural view: God saw what He made and 'behold, it was very good.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Supervision of nude exhibitions
rubrics_metrics.description: "He join'd in defending the exhibition of nude figures, but thought considerable supervision should be exercis'd over such exhibitions."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even proponents of nude art recommend oversight of exhibitions to ensure standards of training, taste, and ethical purpose are maintained.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commemoration of Lincoln's death as national (not sectional) duty
rubrics_metrics.description: "No narrow or sectional reminiscence. It belongs to these States in their entirety--not the North only, but the South--perhaps belongs most tenderly and devoutly to the South..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whitman prescribes annual memorial gatherings marking April 14/15 as a unifying national observance; the lecture advocates remembering Lincoln's death as belonging to the whole country and as a civic and imaginative duty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Great deaths/martyrdom condense nationality and have supreme cultural value
rubrics_metrics.description: "The final use of a heroic-eminent life--especially of a heroic-eminent death--is its indirect filtering into the nation and the race... Then there is a cement to the whole people... namely, the cement of a death identified thoroughly with that people."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whitman asserts a criterion for national culture: dramatic deaths (martyrs, great deaths) are among a nation's most important inheritances, supplying material for literature, drama, and the emotional cohesion of a people; this is a key interpretive lens for historians and artists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historic events acquire highest meaning through dramatic/poetic denouement
rubrics_metrics.description: "A long and varied series of contradictory events arrives at last at its highest poetic, single, central, pictorial denouement... The whole involved, baffling, multiform whirl of the secession period comes to a head, and is gather'd in one brief flash of lightning-illumination--one simple, fierce deed."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whitman emphasizes that the imaginative and dramatic condensation of events (as in Lincoln's murder) is what gives them enduring artistic and historical significance; creators (historians, poets, dramatists) should look for such central pictorial denouements.
